content: 1. Sodium nitrite can cause or significantly contribute to mortality in adults at oral doses as low as 1 gram and intravenous doses as low as 600 milligrams. 2. A fatality attributed to sodium nitrite has been reported in a 17-month-old child following the administration of an adult dose (300 mg intravenously followed by a second dose of 150 mg). 3. Cyanosis may become evident when methemoglobin levels reach 10-20%. 4. Other clinical signs and symptoms of sodium nitrite toxicity, such as anxiety, dyspnea, nausea, and tachycardia, can manifest at methemoglobin levels as low as 15%. 5. More severe signs and symptoms, including cardiac dysrhythmias, circulatory failure, and central nervous system depression, occur as methemoglobin levels increase, with levels above 70% typically being fatal. 6. 7. Severe methemoglobinemia can be treated with intravenous methylene blue, although this treatment may also release cyanide bound to methemoglobin. 8. 9. 10. Cyanide rapidly binds to cytochrome a3, a component of the cytochrome c oxidase complex in mitochondria. 11. Inhibition of cytochrome a3 prevents cells from utilizing oxygen, forcing anaerobic metabolism, which leads to lactate production, cellular hypoxia, and metabolic acidosis. 12. In cases of massive acute cyanide poisoning, other enzyme systems may also be involved in the mechanism of toxicity. 13. The combination of sodium nitrite and sodium thiosulfate as a treatment for cyanide poisoning works synergistically due to differences in their primary mechanisms of action as antidotes. 14. Sodium nitrite exerts its therapeutic effect by reacting with hemoglobin to form methemoglobin, an oxidized form of hemoglobin that cannot transport oxygen but has a high affinity for cyanide. 15. Cyanide preferentially binds to methemoglobin over cytochrome a3, forming the nontoxic compound cyanomethemoglobin. 16. Methemoglobin displaces cyanide from cytochrome oxidase, allowing aerobic metabolism to resume. 17. The chemical reactions involved are as follows: Sodium nitrite reacts with hemoglobin to form methemoglobin. Hydrogen cyanide reacts with methemoglobin to form cyanomethemoglobin. 18. Vasodilation has also been suggested to contribute to the therapeutic effect of sodium nitrite. 19. Sodium nitrite-induced methemoglobinemia may be more effective against cyanide poisoning than comparable levels of methemoglobinemia induced by other oxidants. 20. Sodium nitrite appears to retain some efficacy even when the formation of methemoglobin is inhibited by methylene blue. 21. The primary route of endogenous cyanide detoxification is enzymatic transulfuration to thiocyanate, which is relatively nontoxic and excreted in the urine. 22. Sodium thiosulfate acts as a sulfur donor in the reaction catalyzed by the enzyme rhodanese, enhancing the endogenous detoxification of cyanide. 23. Sodium nitrite has the chemical name nitrous acid sodium salt, with the chemical formula NaNO2 and a molecular weight of 69. 24. Sodium nitrite injection is a sterile aqueous solution intended for intravenous administration, containing 300 mg of sodium nitrite in a 10 mL solution (30 mg/mL) with a pH between 7.0 and 9.0. 25. When 4 mg/kg of sodium nitrite was administered intravenously to six healthy human volunteers, the mean peak methemoglobin concentration was 7%, achieved within 30-60 minutes after injection. 26. 27. Five of the six subjects could not tolerate orthostatic testing due to fainting. 28. One subject who received a 12 mg/kg dose of sodium nitrite experienced severe cardiovascular effects and reached a peak methemoglobin concentration of 30% at 60 minutes post-injection. 29. Oral doses of 120-180 mg of sodium nitrite administered to healthy volunteers caused minimal cardiovascular changes when subjects remained in the horizontal position. However, upon being placed in the upright position, subjects exhibited tachycardia, hypotension, and syncope. 30. The half-life for the conversion of methemoglobin to normal hemoglobin in cyanide poisoning victims treated with sodium nitrite is estimated to be 55 minutes. 31. Sodium nitrite is a strong oxidant that reacts rapidly with hemoglobin to form methemoglobin. 32. Approximately 40% of sodium nitrite is excreted unchanged in the urine, while the remaining 60% is metabolized to ammonia and related small molecules. 33. In patients treated for acute cyanide poisoning with sodium nitrite and sodium thiosulfate, the apparent terminal elimination half-life and volume of distribution of cyanide have been reported to be 19 hours and 0.41 L/kg, respectively. 34. An initial elimination half-life of cyanide has been reported to be approximately 1-3 hours. 35. After detoxification, thiocyanate is excreted primarily in the urine at a rate inversely proportional to creatinine clearance. 36. In healthy subjects, the elimination half-life and volume of distribution of thiocyanate are reported to be 2.7 days and 0.25 L/kg, respectively. However, in individuals with renal insufficiency, the elimination half-life is approximately 9 days. 37. 38. In a 2-year study, sodium nitrite administered orally to rats at doses equivalent to 0, 35, 70, or 130 mg/kg for males and 0, 40, 80, or 150 mg/kg for females did not result in significant increases in tumor incidence. 39. In a similar 2-year study in mice, equivocal results were observed in female mice, with a positive trend toward an increased incidence of squamous cell papilloma or carcinoma in the forestomach. 40. The incidence of hyperplasia of the glandular stomach epithelium was significantly greater in high-dose male mice compared to controls.
